# Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Rheumatology and immunology > Vasculitis > Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis*

[Original Article Link](/library/At0RT3)

---

## Summary

Cutaneous <u>small-vessel vasculitis</u> is a <u>non-ANCA-associated vasculitis of small vessels</u> that affects the <u>skin</u>; involvement of other organs must be absent. Cutaneous <u>small-vessel vasculitis</u> is often <u>idiopathic</u>, but all patients should be evaluated for potential underlying causes, including infections (e.g., <u>HIV</u>, <u>HCV</u>), the use of certain drugs (e.g., <u>propylthiouracil</u>, <u>hydralazine</u>, <u>allopurinol</u>), and other <u>vasculitides</u> (e.g., <u>eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis</u>). Patients usually present with tender, symmetrical palpable <u>purpura</u> on the lower limbs. <u>Skin biopsy</u> is required to confirm the diagnosis; findings include <u>leukocytoclastic vasculitis</u>. Management depends on the severity and chronicity of the lesions, but <u>NSAIDs</u> and bed rest are usually recommended. <u>Glucocorticoids</u> may be indicated in patients with severe, recurrent, or chronic disease.

---

## Definitions

A necrotizing <u>vasculitis</u> of cutaneous small vessels caused by <u>immune complex</u> deposition; involvement of organs other than the <u>skin</u> must be absent.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Idiopathic</u> in 45–55% of cases [[2]](/library/C-Xqz00)[[3]](/library/x-XEz00)

* Potential causes include:

* Autoimmune diseases (e.g., <u>SLE</u>, <u>ANCA vasculitis</u>)

* Infections (e.g., <u>HIV</u>, <u>HCV</u>)

* Use of certain drugs (e.g., <u>propylthiouracil</u>, <u>hydralazine</u>, <u>allopurinol</u>, <u>penicillins</u>, <u>cephalosporin</u>, <u>sulfasalazine</u>, <u>phenytoin</u>)





> [!TIP]
> Patients may report flare triggers such as prolonged sitting or standing, <u>alcohol</u> consumption, or <u>URTIs</u>. [[2]](/library/C-Xqz00)

---

## Clinical features

* Painful, symmetric nonblanching palpable <u>purpura</u> on the lower limbs [[2]](/library/C-Xqz00)

* Other lesions: subcutaneous <u>nodules</u>, <u>urticaria</u>, <u>ulcers</u>, <u>vesicles</u>

* <u>Arthralgias</u> may be present.





> [!TIP]
> If drug-induced, lesions usually appear 7–10 days after exposure.

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[2]](/library/C-Xqz00)[[3]](/library/x-XEz00)




* Consult dermatology and/or rheumatology.

* Request additional diagnostics to: 

* Investigate the underlying etiology

* Rule out systemic <u>vasculitis</u>

* A <u>skin biopsy</u> is needed to confirm the diagnosis.





> [!TIP]
> If lesions are confined to a single location, consider a local factor (e.g., trauma, an <u>insect bite</u>) as the underlying etiology. [[2]](/library/C-Xqz00)




### <u>Skin biopsy</u>




* Indication: Obtain for all patients to confirm the diagnosis.

* Findings: <u>leukocytoclastic vasculitis</u>  [[2]](/library/C-Xqz00)[[4]](/library/U30b3f)

* Perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate of <u>postcapillary venules</u>

* Fibrinoid deposits





> [!TIP]
> The pathological mechanism that causes cutaneous <u>small-vessel vasculitis</u> can also cause <u>vasculitides</u> in organs other than the <u>skin</u>, which are categorized as distinct diseases. A <u>skin biopsy</u> is essential to establish a definite diagnosis. [[2]](/library/C-Xqz00)
